docs.title: About the lab
docs.text:
We use state-of-the-art approaches to study the neural mechanisms that underlie adaptive control of behavior in animals.

Learn more →

docs.title: Recruitment
docs.text:
Our members come from a wide range of backgrounds and work together toward a common goal: understanding how the brain works. We are broadly recruiting graduate students and research staff.

E-mail: kitamurak [at] yamanashi.ac.jp

docs.title: Graduate Students (Master's and Doctoral)
docs.text:
We welcome motivated students with an interest in neuroscience, whatever their undergraduate background. Research supervision is tailored to each individual, whether their strengths lie in experiments or in analysis. Students can be admitted through the Master's Program in Biomedical Sciences, the three-year Doctoral Program in Integrated Applied Life Sciences, or the four-year Doctoral Program in Medicine.

  • No prior background in neuroscience is required; you can start learning it after entering graduate school
  • Active support for students aiming at a research career
  • Support for career development, including employment in industry
  • Information available on RA/TA positions and financial support schemes for doctoral students
  • Consultation on JSPS DC fellowship applications and acceptance is welcome at any time

docs.title: Research Staff
docs.text:
We are recruiting postdoctoral researchers. Experience in the following areas is particularly welcome.

  • Electrophysiology (patch clamp, in vivo unit recording)
  • Imaging (calcium imaging, in vivo imaging)
  • Behavioral experiments in rats and mice
  • Data analysis and theoretical modeling
  • Image processing, machine learning and AI
  • Molecular biology and gene transfer
  • Histology and immunostaining

Enquiries regarding JSPS PD and RPD fellowships and JSPS International Postdoctoral Fellowships are also welcome.

docs.title: Graduate Students / Postdocs
docs.text: Motivated graduate students and postdoctoral researchers from diverse backgrounds are welcome. Electrophysiology, calcium imaging, behavior, data analysis, molecular biology and morphology are all useful experience, and applicants from other disciplines are equally welcome.

docs.title: Research Interests
docs.text:
Markerless body-part tracking in a behaving mouse Two-photon calcium imaging of cerebellar Purkinje cells Wide-field calcium imaging

We use optical and electrophysiological techniques in behaving animals to elucidate the mechanisms of sensorimotor information processing in the brain. We are particularly interested in understanding the role of the cerebellum and related brain regions in adaptive behavioral control.

docs.title: Research themes
docs.text:
• Motor control and learning mechanisms by cerebro-cerebellar loop
  • Physiological relevance of diverse information coding in the cerebellum
  • Information flow from decision-making to behavior output
  • Mechanism of auditory perception in the cortex

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text:
• Calcium Imaging (two-photon, single-photon)
  • Electrophysiology (multi-unit recordings, patch-clamp)
  • Optogenetics
  • Development of novel behavioral tasks for rodents
  • Image processing, machine learning and AI

docs.title: Recent Papers
docs.text:
• Yokoyama et al., Nat. Methods, 2024

    A multicolor suite for deciphering population coding of calcium and cAMP in vivo.

    Development of the red calcium sensor RCaMP3 and the green cAMP sensor cAMPinG1. A collaboration with Dr. Sakamoto and colleagues at Kyoto University.

  • Mochizuki et al., Sci. Rep., 2024

    Optogenetic stimulation of neurons in the anterior cingulate cortex induces changes in intravesical bladder pressure and the micturition reflex.

    A novel mechanism by which the anterior cingulate cortex controls bladder contraction and micturition. A collaboration with the Department of Urology.

  • Ikezoe, Hidaka et al., Commun. Biol., 2023

    Cerebellar climbing fibers multiplex movement and reward signals during a voluntary movement task in mice.

    We show that climbing fibers multiplex diverse movement and reward information and convey it to the cerebellum.
